name: Bengt Ankarloo
specialization: Scandinavian witchcraft; comparative European witch-hunting; editorial and synthesis work

major_works.title: Witchcraft and Magic in Europe (6 volumes, co-editor with Stuart Clark)
major_works.significance: Definitive comparative survey of European witchcraft and magic across all periods; made regional scholarship accessible in synthesis form

major_works.title: Trolldomsprocesserna i Sverige (Witchcraft Trials in Sweden)
major_works.significance: Foundational study of Swedish witchcraft prosecutions using legal records; established Scandinavian regional witchcraft historiography

core_argument: Scandinavian witchcraft prosecutions, while sharing structural features with Central European patterns, had distinctive characteristics shaped by Lutheran state-churches, late timing of major panics (1660s-1670s in Sweden), and different legal procedures. Comparative European perspective is essential: no single regional pattern can stand as the norm for European witch-hunting.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Swedish legal and church records; Scandinavian regional trial documentation
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Regional prosecution patterns in Scandinavia; comparative European framework for contextualizing local studies
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Archival legal history; comparative synthesis of regional studies across Europe
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Regional comparative: identifying structural similarities and differences across European jurisdictions

key_contributions.claim: Sweden and other Scandinavian countries had major witch panics (notably 1668-1676 Dalarna panic) with distinctive features, including children as accusers and high execution rates
key_contributions.implication: Scandinavian data challenges models built only on German, French, or English cases

key_contributions.claim: No single regional experience is typical; European witch-hunting must be understood through systematic comparison
key_contributions.implication: The six-volume Witchcraft and Magic in Europe series provides the comparative infrastructure for such analysis

key_contributions.claim: Making disparate regional scholarship available in translation and synthesis is itself a scholarly contribution
key_contributions.implication: Ankarloo's collaboration with Clark demonstrates that scholarly infrastructure (edited volumes, translations) shapes how fields develop

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Swedish legal history tradition; comparative European social history; collaboration with Stuart Clark
criticisms: Primary work in Swedish has limited accessibility to non-Scandinavian scholars
As primarily an editorial synthesizer, his individual theoretical contributions are less prominent than his collaborative work

historiographical_significance: Ankarloo made Scandinavian witchcraft scholarship internationally accessible and, through co-editing the six-volume Witchcraft and Magic in Europe with Stuart Clark, created the most comprehensive comparative reference work in the field. His regional expertise on Swedish prosecutions established Scandinavian witchcraft as a distinct area of inquiry. His collaboration with Clark bridged intellectual history and regional social history approaches.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
